definitions.definition: Network of everyday physical things embedded with electronics, software and sensors, connected to the internet to exchange data and enable monitoring and control.
Machine-to-Machine: networking of machines or devices for the purpose of remote monitoring, control and data exchange.
Network of interconnected devices, objects, people and processes that communicate to collect and exchange data; built from devices, sensors, networks, cloud platforms and applications.
Physical device that passes data streams from sensors to the cloud and back, performing data preprocessing before transfer to the cloud.
Platform where IoT solutions can be bought or obtained free, offering hardware, specialized software, applications or complete hardware-software-cloud packages.
Cisco's seven-level reference model: physical devices, connectivity, edge computing, data accumulation, data abstraction, application, and collaboration and processes.
Level 3 of the Cisco IoT model that receives packets and outputs data understandable to higher levels, performing filtering, aggregation and packet content inspection.
Data analysis tool that assesses the wide range of data collected from IoT devices and produces useful information, without extra hardware or infrastructure.
Device that transforms energy from one form to another, e.g. a microphone converting sound into electrical energy.
Device that detects changes and events in a physical environment and converts physical parameters like temperature, pressure and motion into electrical signals.
Device that changes electrical signals into mechanical work, used to cause movement or a change in the surroundings.
Sensor whose response depends on the magnitude, direction and orientation of the input parameter, e.g. accelerometer, gyroscope and motion detector.
Passive infrared electronic sensor that measures IR light radiating from objects in its field of view; mainly used for detecting human motion.
Device that uses pressurized fluid in a cylinder or motor to perform mechanical work and can generate large force.
Actuator that converts energy produced by vacuum or compressed air at high pressure into linear or rotary motion.
Hardware and software combination integrated into a single platform to perform specific functions or control within a larger system.
Open-source electronic prototyping platform based on programmable microcontroller boards and flexible, easy-to-use hardware and software.
Program code written in the Arduino IDE, divided into setup() for initialization and loop() for iterating the specified task.
Synchronous serial data protocol used by microcontrollers to communicate with one or more peripherals quickly over short distances, using CIPO, COPI, SCK and CS lines.
Raspberry Pi interface that allows synchronous data transfer with just two pins: SDA (data line) and SCL (clock line).
Open-source, Linux-based credit-card-sized computer board that interfaces sensors and actuators through GPIO pins.
Generic pin on the Raspberry Pi, controlled by the user at run time for input or output; the board exposes 40 such pins.
Microcontroller board based on the Intel Quark SoC X1000, a 32-bit Pentium-class SoC, pin-compatible with Arduino UNO R3 shields.
Low-cost digital sensor that measures relative humidity and temperature using a capacitive humidity element and a negative-temperature-coefficient thermistor.
Very small Wi-Fi development kit with a 120 MHz ARM Cortex-M3 microcontroller and on-board Broadcom Wi-Fi chip for connected IoT projects.
Infrastructure-less wireless network with a large number of wireless sensors deployed in an ad-hoc manner to monitor system, physical or environmental conditions.
Central node of a WSN that collects and processes data from sensor nodes and transmits it through the internet to a remote server.
Low-energy clustering protocol for wireless sensor networks that groups nodes into clusters and rotates the cluster-head role to save energy.
Fundamental WSN problem that reflects the quality of service that can be provided by a particular sensor network.
Topology with a single central node (hub) to which every node connects; a failure in the hub can result in failure of the entire network.
Arrangement in which each node also relays other nodes' data; fully connected form links every node, partial form links only neighbours.
IEEE 802.11 wireless networking technology that uses high-frequency radio waves instead of cables to connect devices to a LAN and the internet.
Group of stations communicating at the physical layer, either through an access point or peer-to-peer in an ad-hoc manner.
Short-range wireless communications technology, invented by Ericsson in 1994, that replaces cables between portable units using ad-hoc piconets.
Small Bluetooth network formed by at most 8 stations: one master node managing up to 7 slave nodes, plus up to 255 parked nodes.
Interconnected collection of two or more piconets, formed through a bridge node that acts as a member of two piconets.
Low-power, low-data-rate WPAN specification developed under IEEE 802.15.4 for connecting many battery-powered control and sensor devices.
Mains-powered device, one per Zigbee network, that starts and maintains the network, selects its security mode and bridges data to the home network.
Long Range Radio: wireless protocol developed by Semtech for long-range, low-power communications, mainly targeted at M2M and IoT networks.
Short-range communication standard, based on RFID, enabling compatible devices to transmit data over radio waves.
